abstract: The routine generation of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic data from the same biological system has turned multi-omics integration from a methodological aspiration into a daily expectation, yet the software landscape answering this demand is fragmented across unsupervised factor-analytic engines, supervised discriminant frameworks, deep representation-learning architectures, pathway-aware aggregators, microbiome-native pipelines and graphical web platforms. This review applies a common set of criteria—input data structures, handling of missingness, supervision regime, scalability, biological target, reproducibility infrastructure and empirical benchmarking—to a curated set of frameworks, packages, workflows and platforms, organised along three axes: the stage at which integration is performed (early, intermediate or late), the degree of supervision required, and the biological question being addressed. We critically discuss general-purpose Bioconductor frameworks such as MultiAssayExperiment, mixOmics, MOFA and pathwayMultiomics; microbiome-centred tools including gNOMO, gNOMO2, PALM and EasyMultiProfiler; and point-and-click platforms such as Profiler, ExpOmics, ExpressVis, the Analyst ecosystem and MONGKIE. EasyMultiProfiler, an R workflow built on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment and organised into extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation modules, is featured as an example of microbiome-centred workflow design that aligns host and microbial assays within standardised data structures. We argue that the field's binding constraint is no longer algorithmic novelty but the absence of shared benchmarks, ground-truth corpora and FAIR-compliant evaluation infrastructure; claims of superiority should therefore be read with caution, and progress will depend less on yet another statistical engine than on reproducible, microbiome-native assessment.
